title: Sanitation services for the urban poor: A social capital approach to sanitation challenges in informal settlements
authors: Chumo I.; Mberu B.; Wainaina C.; Murigi W.; Sumba L.; Kabaria C.
notes: Qualitative content-analysis study of sanitation-access challenges among manual pit emptiers and community members (24 FGDs, 14 IDIs, n approx 250) in Korogocho and Viwandani informal settlements, Nairobi, Kenya. Distinguishes challenges outside the household (legislative, physical, social) from challenges at the household level (health, financial, technical). authors: Caldera Ortega A.R.; Tagle Zamora D.
notes: Political-ecology/institutional evaluation of the 30-year drinking water and sewerage concession granted to a private company (later Veolia/CAASA) in Aguascalientes, Mexico, and its 2023 remunicipalization. (S035) and Fracalanza et al. -- documentary/institutional evidence combined with real official household indicators tied to a specific legal/contractual framework.

title: Water scarcity and excess: water insecurity in cities of Nepal
authors: Maskey G.; Pandey C.L.; Giri M.
notes: Qualitative study (40 key informant interviews, informal conversations, observations, 2020-2021) of household-level water insecurity in three Nepali municipalities (Dharan, Dhulikhel, Khairahani). Documents household-level formal connection and administrative barriers: Dhulikhel's 'one-house-one-tap' municipal connection policy vs. peripheral/annexed wards and Chaudhari communities not yet reached by water connections; of 36,000 households in Dharan, 10,000 depend on unsafe water sources; slum settlements in Dharan unable to afford piped water connections (BURDEN/fees, ELIGIBILITY/service_area mechanisms); Dharan Municipality building-permit subsidy conditioned on rainwater-harvesting/recharge-pit construction (BURDEN/documentation, property mechanism); institutional fragmentation among NWSC, Water Board, Water Users Committee, and municipal governments. Qualitative socio-legal study; included per standing rule on qualitative studies. Flags sibling Nepal water-governance paper by overlapping author (Maskey G.) in the pool, unscreened: RE3D6C0549F37 (Bhattarai et al., gender inequality in urban water governance, Nepal).

title: Sanitation challenges in Dar es Salaam: the potential of Simplified Sewerage Systems
authors: Yap C.; Mcfarlane C.; Ndezi T.; Makoba F.D.
notes: Mixed-methods household survey (n=104 households, of 300 houses connected to a Simplified Sewerage System/SSS) plus focus group discussions in Mji Mpya informal settlement, Dar es Salaam, Tanzania. Documents a household-level BURDEN/affordability mechanism: SSS connection and ongoing costs are distributed unevenly between tenants and landlords, with tenants at risk of bearing costs landlords pass on via rent/contracts absent 'simple regulations across homes'; authors recommend identifying households needing subsidies (large families, lowest-income tenants) in tariff design. Also documents an ENFORCEMENT mechanism: fines for illegal pit-latrine waste disposal. Mixed-tenure context explicitly discussed as shaping differential access/cost outcomes.

title: Affordability of household water services across the United States
authors: Patterson L.A.; Bryson S.A.; Doyle M.W.
notes: Large-N quantitative study of household water tariff affordability across 787 of the largest U.S. drinking water utilities (one representative utility per state where possible), combining manually-collected water/wastewater rate structures with service-area-level census income data. Defines undue hardship as paying >4.6% of household income for 6,000 gallons/month; finds 17% of households (28.3 million persons) face unaffordable basic water bills, with the median community having 1-in-7 households above this threshold. Documents BURDEN mechanism (tariff/rate-structure variation shaped by differing state legislation and regulations) and the ENFORCEMENT/disconnection consequence of nonpayment (loss of access via shut-offs), plus the ELIGIBILITY/DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION landscape of local customer assistance programs (CAPs, not consistently available). Strong candidate for quantitative synthesis given the large N and standardized affordability metric across many jurisdictions.

title: Examining liveability in the informal community of Kabawa, Nigeria
authors: Obayomi A.; Popoola A.; Medayese S.; Wahab B.
notes: Mixed-methods household survey (structured questionnaire, observation checklist, housing facility survey; n=180 household heads) in Kabawa, an informal settlement in Lokoja, Kogi State, Nigeria. Household-level water/sanitation access data: 17.2% no toilet facility, 11.7% pour-flush, 7.8% pipe-borne water connection, 13.9% boreholes, 18.3% soak-away. Documents a DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION/participation mechanism: residents report 'governance exclusion' -- local and state governments never involved them in development decision-making or considered them in provision of basic facilities (direct interview quotes from a youth leader and community leader). Also documents institutional fragmentation between a Federal Government constituency-project solar-powered water facility (free, community-maintained, in good condition) and the unreliable, poorly-maintained Kogi State Water Board pipe-borne supply.

title: Sharing Difficult Waters: Community-Based Groundwater Recharge and Use in Algeria and India
authors: Saidani M.A.; Aslekar U.; Kuper M.; Kemerink-Seyoum J.
notes: Qualitative fieldwork case study of two community-based groundwater recharge/domestic-water systems: Beni Isguen (M'Zab Valley, Algeria) and Randullabad (Maharashtra, India). Documents an ELIGIBILITY/legal-status mechanism directly on point: the customary water-governance organisation (Umana Essayl) 'has no legal status in the eyes of the state,' limiting its ability to access formal financial support despite the state recognising its societal role and importance -- a community created a formal association specifically to try to qualify for state funding, with only partial success. Also documents the state-led development of drinking water/sanitation networks now delivering water directly to households (replacing traditional systems), and in the India case a Village Watershed Committee-built piped distribution system giving every household tap water on an alternate-day schedule, governed by locally-set well-siting/depth/pump-capacity regulations. Qualitative socio-legal study; included per standing rule that qualitative studies are not excluded for lacking a quantitative effect size.

title: Disparities in Drinking Water and Sanitation in the Urban Slums of Kerala, India
authors: Vidhyadharan A.
notes: Quantitative comparative household survey of two urban slums in Kerala, India (Vizhinjam vs Barten Hill), using water/sanitation deprivation indices, chi-square, t-test, and Mann-Whitney U tests (e.g. Mann-Whitney U=3742, p<0.05 for wastewater disposal difference). Documents a BURDEN/fees mechanism: households with a Kerala Water Authority (KWA) piped connection pay a water charge, those using public taps/protected wells pay nothing, and those relying on private tanker lorries (common in the more-deprived Vizhinjam) pay private-market prices, creating an affordability gap; 3.6% of Vizhinjam households additionally must pay for community toilets (no exclusive-use option), unlike the free community toilets used elsewhere. Below-poverty-line (BPL) status used as an income/eligibility marker distinguishing the two slum populations. Strong quantitative comparative study with real statistical effect estimates directly on point for the review's Family A/C interest in legal/administrative barriers and access inequality.

title: Faecal sludge emptying in Sub-Saharan Africa, South and Southeast Asia: A systematic review of emptying technology choices, challenges, and improvement initiatives
authors: Muoghalu C.; Semiyaga S.; Manga M.
notes: This is itself a systematic review (37 primary studies, Jan 2002-Dec 2021) of faecal sludge (FS) emptying in Sub-Saharan Africa, South and Southeast Asia -- per RISK_OF_BIAS.md Section 1, appraise with AMSTAR 2 (not a primary-study tool) and flag in evidence_map.csv as study_design_class=systematic_review_secondary so it is never treated as an independent primary effect for pooling. Directly relevant to the review's household-level sanitation-access-mechanism scope: documents real household-level cost/BURDEN barriers (mechanical pit-emptying reported up to 4x more costly than manual emptying; households with accessible plots/service availability pay markedly less, per Jenkins et al. 2015 Tanzania finding cited in the review), a documented ENFORCEMENT mechanism (illegal FS dumping/disposal explicitly outlawed in India, Kenya, and Ghana per reviewed studies), and licenses/permits governing formal emptying operations plus 'inadequate sanitation-related regulations' and lack of enforcement capacity identified as a recurring institutional barrier across the reviewed literature. Belongs to the fecal-sludge-management (FSM) cluster previously flagged during earlier screening (Basnet & Sherchan, Ilangovan et al., and Fanaian et al. are the other systematic-review-secondary studies already included in this pool).

title: Equity dimensions in initiatives promoting urban health and wellbeing in east and southern Africa
authors: Loewenson R.; Mhlanga G.; Gotto D.; Chayikosa S.; Goma F.; Walyaro C.
notes: Thematic analysis (52 documents + 10 primary case studies from Harare, Kampala, Lusaka, Nairobi) of urban health-equity initiatives in east/southern Africa. Multi-sector scope (water, sanitation, waste, food security, working/environmental conditions, health systems) -- borderline like Nurmaningtyas et al. (S004), but water/sanitation content is substantive and directly relevant: a dedicated case-study theme on 'Community-led water and sanitation response in informal settlements' (Table 3), the Epworth (peri-urban Harare) case of joint community-authority water-quality monitoring and management of water/sanitation systems, a water-conserving toilet innovation scaled via a community lending group, and SDI/Muungano wa Wanavijiji's use of a 'right to the city' lens to map rights violations and duty-bearer deficits in Nairobi informal settlements (a DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION/participation and legal-recognition mechanism). Also documents 'contested land, lacking legal title undermined security of tenure' (Hatcliffe urban agriculture case) as a general tenure-insecurity theme in the same urban-informality context. Only the water/sanitation-specific portions are relevant for extraction -- same practice as the Torres-Sandoval et al. (S022) Mexico survey, which also covered multiple services jointly. Note for extraction: this functions partly as a review of 52 secondary documents and partly as a primary 10-case qualitative study; study_design_class should be resolved at extraction (not automatically systematic_review_secondary, since it also reports primary case-study fieldwork).

title: Arsenic in Philippine Groundwaters: Exploring Governance Limitations for Drinking Water Safety
authors: Faulmino C.J.P.; Rola A.C.
notes: Documentary/institutional legal analysis (textual analysis of legal documents and official reports, plus roundtable/meeting transcripts with national agency representatives) of the Philippine legal-regulatory framework for arsenic risk management in drinking water, mapped 'source-to-sip.' Directly on point: finds the country's legal framework (LWUA and water districts regulated under Executive Order No. 124 of 1987; Rural Waterworks and Sanitation Associations; Certificate of Potability of Drinking Water requirement) provides functioning arsenic-mitigation coverage for formal, regulated water supplies (ELIGIBILITY/service_area mechanism) but 'fails to protect self-provisioning households as they access water from informal systems uncovered by water quality surveillance' -- a clear ENFORCEMENT/coverage gap disadvantaging households outside the formal regulatory net. Includes real case data (e.g. a municipality of 128,893 population with only 13% covered by the local Water District). risk_of_bias_tool for eventual extraction: Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework.

title: Sanitation strategies for reducing open defecation in rural areas of India and Ethiopia
authors: Humňalová H.; Ficek F.
notes: Comparative country-level policy analysis (India SBM vs Ethiopia CLTS): legal grounding (both lack enforceable sanitation right), financing/subsidy mechanisms (ELIGIBILITY/BURDEN), enforcement (ENFORCEMENT: fines/arrests/ration withdrawal for non-compliance), and household-level outcome data (Tab.1-2: toilet coverage / OD rate change 2000-2020 by country). Doctrinal/institutional comparative synthesis with real empirical outcome data, same category as previously-included country-policy pieces (Murthy, Fanaian, Muller).

title: Perspectives from the Ground: Governing Informality of Water in Metro Manila
authors: Hussain N.; Chaves C.
notes: Mixed-methods case study (household survey n=800, FGDs n=9, semi-structured interviews n=70) of legal/administrative mechanisms shaping household water access in Metro Manila informal settlements/resettlement sites. Examines ELIGIBILITY (land title/lease-contract requirement for connection applications; concessionaire right-of-way refusal in disputed-tenure areas), BURDEN (cooperative-formation costs/barriers), ENFORCEMENT (National Water Crisis Act 1995 criminalizing water pilferage/resale -- fines/imprisonment), and administrative discretion (Urban Development and Housing Act RA 7279 minimum-compliance implementation). Outcomes: primary_connection (piped-into-dwelling vs shared/vendor share of Fig.2), economic_access (4-12% income spent on water, Table 1), effective_access (87% households report shortages, Table 2, with significance tests).

title: Environmental Injustice and Marginalization: Water Lack of Access in the Metropolitan Zone of the Valley of Mexico; [Injustiça ambiental e marginalização: a falta de acesso à água na Área Metropolitana do Vale do México]; [Injusticia ambiental y marginación: la falta de acceso al agua en la Zona Metropolitana del Valle de México]
authors: Pastrana-Miranda T.; González-Caamal M.M.
notes: Qualitative/documentary institutional case study (Ecatepec, State of Mexico, within the Metropolitan Zone of the Valley of Mexico) using neo-institutional analysis and a hemerographic protest review (Table 1, 2018-2020) plus real INEGI census statistics (2015 Encuesta Intercensal: 81.39% ZMVM households with in-home water access; >60% lacking water in 15 State of Mexico municipios). Documents DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION/political clientelism (water distribution tied to electoral cycles and party affiliation of municipal government -- CAEM/SAPASE institutional tension), institutional fragmentation across federal/state/municipal water governance (centralization-to-municipalization history), and a household-level primary_connection/service_coverage outcome (in-home piped water access by municipality).

title: Coping Strategies, Cultural Practices and Policy Implications on Domestic Water Supply in an Erosion Susceptible Rural Community, Nigeria
authors: Ezeudu O.B.; Ezeudu T.S.; Ugochukwu U.C.; Okolo O.J.; Ani C.D.; Ajogu A.P.; Ajaero C.C.; Mbakwe U.I.; Nduji N.N.
notes: Qualitative case study (in-depth semi-structured interviews, >30-45 participants, purposive sampling, plus documented evidence and field observation) of domestic water coping strategies in Nanka, an erosion-susceptible rural community in Anambra State, Nigeria. Examines institutional/governance mechanisms: tripartite federal/state/local government water-responsibility division, Federal Ministry of Water Resources policy/legislation/regulation authority, state water boards' regulatory role over private providers, and documents 'absent and nonfunctional water institutions' and 'poor water policy implementation' as key drivers of inadequate rural water supply. Outcome: household-level water access/coping (sources, practices, barriers) in a rural community lacking piped/improved water infrastructure.

title: The limits of insulation: The long-term political dynamics of public–private service delivery
authors: Cruxên I.A.
notes: Comparative historical case study (interviews + company/regulatory data, 1998-2016) of two mixed public-private water/sanitation utilities in Brazil (Copasa/Minas Gerais, Sanepar/Parana), examining how political modulation by state-government-appointed managers shapes service-delivery direction. Documents real institutional/governance mechanisms: tariff policy (social tariff for low-income affordability at Sanepar; multi-year tariff freezes by the governor absent an independent regulatory agency; later ARSAE regulatory tariff-setting at Copasa) -- BURDEN/economic_access; targeted coverage-expansion programs to poor/rural areas (25,000 rural Parana households; a Copasa subsidiary targeting low-income areas) -- primary_connection/service_coverage; and disconnection-to-non-payers pressure under market-oriented management -- ENFORCEMENT. Real utility metrics: connections-per-thousand dropped from 3.13 (1999); R45 million 2002 revenue; 16% tariff increase (2011).

title: Laying Bare: Determinants of Informal Water Vendors for Domestic Water Supply in Himalayan Mountain Towns
authors: Shah R.
notes: Qualitative fieldwork (2014-2019; household survey n=149 across 29 wards, stratified + snowball sampling; topic-guided stakeholder interviews) on informal water vendors and formal-system disconnection in Darjeeling, India. Strong ELIGIBILITY mechanism: legality of residence required to even apply for a municipal water connection -- unregistered residences are ineligible to submit a private-connection application and receive only public-tap access instead of household-level connections. Documents BURDEN (documentation, high costs, lengthy bureaucratic application process requiring personal 'connections and networks' to move through the municipal office) and DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION/malgovernance (political patronage networks, dissolved elected municipal bodies during statehood agitation periods, corrupt tender/fund allocation). Outcome: only 10-15% of Darjeeling households receive municipal water supply; 85% depend on informal vendors/community springs.

title: The action of Obras Sanitarias de la Nación in Mendoza: infrastructure and sanitation between agreements and conflicts (1918-1928); [La acción de Obras Sanitarias de la Nación en Mendoza: infraestructura y saneamiento entre acuerdos y conflictos (1918-1928)]
authors: Luis N.; Raffa C.
notes: Historical archival case study (primary sources: local press, provincial executive official documents, national agency graphic records, legislative session diaries) of Obras Sanitarias de la Nacion (OSN, Argentina's federal sanitary works agency) governance in Mendoza province, 1918-1928. Examines institutional_fragmentation via the 1900 law (Ley 3967) transferring water/sanitation jurisdiction from provincial to federal control, the 1912 law (Ley 8889) creating OSN, and the recurring federal interventions (4 in the decade) disrupting provincial governance continuity and connection-installation agreements between OSN and provincial/municipal authorities. Reports real household-level connection outcome data across the period: 3,981 domiciliary water connections in 1914 (3,791 Capital + 190 Godoy Cruz); 1,125 domiciliary installations later (90% growth); 710 domiciliary sewer connections by 1927; province-wide OSN connections reaching 8,017 by 1928 (including 831 new connections in San Rafael); 57,500 of 70,500 inhabitants served in one department.

title: How a water trucking governance mechanism in the West Bank enhances equity and sustainability
authors: Cesari G.; Johnson S.O.; Cancelliere G.; Von Medeazza G.
notes: Practice paper documenting the GVC/UNICEF water-trucking subsidy programme in Oslo Accord Area C, West Bank. Directly examines legal/administrative/political mechanisms: Oslo Accords II zoning (Area C under full Israeli control, infrastructure at high risk of demolition, obstructing formal connection funding), Palestinian Water Authority (PWA)-governed multilevel water-trucking governance system, and explicit programme ELIGIBILITY criteria (household water consumption <30 l/capita/day and/or private market price >NIS 20/m3, jointly agreed by PWA/UNICEF/WASH cluster/Water Scarcity Task Force). Real official statistics: 11,000 unserved Palestinians in Area C paying up to 5/m3 (10x the Area A/B public rate of ~.50-6/m3); 153,000 unconnected to the water network; 270,000 with inadequate WASH access; programme reached 35,000 people by 2022. Note: duplicate Scopus record RD9FA1D5723A2 (DOI 10.3362/1756-3488.18-00036, year 2019, no 'OA' suffix) appears to be an earlier non-final DOI for this same article -- marked as duplicate per REPRODUCIBILITY.md S6, cross-referenced to this record.

title: Assessing the Climate Resilience of Community‐Managed Water Supplies in Ethiopia and Nepal
authors: Nijhawan A.; Howard G.; Poudel M.; Pregnolato M.; Lo Y.T.E.; Ghimire A.; Baidya M.; Geremew A.; Flint A.; Mulugeta Y.
notes: Longitudinal field study (Nov 2019-Aug 2021, 20 rural communities in Ethiopia, 15 in Nepal) applying the 'How Tough is WASH' climate-resilience framework, scored via community discussions and technical assessment across six domains including institutional support and community governance. While the central research question is validating the resilience-assessment tool, the field findings document a real BURDEN/economic_access mechanism: Nepal's federal drinking water policy requires user groups to contribute 20-30% of project construction cost, and in one documented community the municipal piped-water supply was recently expanded but the user tariff and new-connection cost were unaffordable for several residents, who continued relying on unsafe boreholes. Also documents institutional_fragmentation (Nepal's federalization creating confusion over which government level -- federal/provincial/local -- is responsible for WUSC oversight) and a DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION/participation gap in Ethiopia (a school board and kebele administration selected a WASH committee without resident input or an engagement channel).

title: Governance drivers of rural water sustainability: Collaboration in frontline service delivery
authors: Thapa D.; Farid M.N.; Prevost C.
notes: Mixed-methods World Bank study (10-year panel data + qualitative outlier case studies) of Indonesia's PAMSIMAS community-based rural water program. Examines institutional/governance mechanisms: frontline state-society relations between village authorities and water user groups, village-authority resource mobilization and bureaucratic support (or its absence) for community water management, and local governance capacity. Real quantitative findings (regression on 10-year panel of water-point functionality) plus qualitative process-tracing of positive/negative deviant villages explaining WHY collaborative vs. unsupportive frontline relations produce sustained vs. abandoned community water systems. Outcome: water-system functionality/sustainability over a 10-year horizon (effective_access/service_continuity). Note: duplicate ProQuest record R346D1BF8F31D (2021, no DOI, likely an earlier working-paper version) found -- marked E08, cross-referenced to this record.

title: Public procurement law, political economy of the lowest responsive bidding, and the development of the water, sanitation and hygiene sector in Nigeria; [Le droit des marchés publics, l’économie politique de l’appel d’offre le moins disant, et le développement du secteur de l’eau, de l’assainissement et de l’hygiène au Nigeria]
authors: Okolie A.-M.; Nnamani K.E.; Nwangwu C.; Agbo H.N.; Cyril Ike C.
notes: Political-economy/doctrinal analysis (secondary data, policy appraisal, and field observation by the authors as UNICEF procurement consultants) of Nigeria's Public Procurement Act 2007 (PPA) and its 'lowest responsive bidding' provision, examining how elite capture of this legal mechanism undermines WASH infrastructure delivery. Documents ENFORCEMENT/regulatory-capture mechanism with concrete case examples: contractors in Benue State incurring cost overruns on a project subsequently awarded only N2.7 million; a state commissioner's account of WASH contracts worth over N800 million awarded to politically-connected contractors who were paid and then abandoned school water/sanitation projects; similar documented cases in Bayelsa, Anambra, and Akwa Ibom states. National outcome statistics tied to this institutional failure: only 68% of Nigerians have basic water access, 19% improved sanitation, 47 million practice open defecation (UNICEF 2014-2017 data); national diarrhoea prevalence rose from 10.2% (2013) to 12.8% (2018).

title: The potential for scaling up container-based sanitation in informal settlements in Kenya
authors: Mallory A.; Mdee A.; Agol D.; Hyde-Smith L.; Kiogora D.; Riungu J.; Parker A.
notes: Political-economy qualitative case study (Jan-Mar 2020 fieldwork; ~59 semi-structured interviews/focus groups with utility employees, sanitation-enterprise staff, NGO employees, public health officers, manual pit emptiers, vacuum truck operators, and national/county government officials; snowball sampling to saturation; NVivo thematic coding) of two container-based sanitation enterprises in Kenya's informal settlements (Nairobi, Naivasha). Documents severe institutional_fragmentation (conflicting 2002 vs. 2016 Water Acts on sanitation mandate, unclear national/county accountability), a real constitutional ELIGIBILITY/enforcement finding (Kenya's 2010 Constitution Article 43 right to sanitation; only one successful court case invoking it in 10 years -- a highways-authority case with a clear duty-bearer), and a documented DISCONNECTION/judicial_review case (Garissa: forcible eviction of 2,000 informal-settlement residents declared unconstitutional, with disconnection from existing water/sanitation services part of the claim). Also documents land-tenure/settlement-'illegality' barriers to service investment by governments/utilities.

title: Policies and incentives for developing universal access to water and sanitation for vulnerable families
authors: Narzetti D.A.; Marques R.C.
notes: Doctrinal/policy analysis of Brazil's legal and regulatory framework for universal water/sanitation access (WSS), centered on Law 11.445 (2007) -- the national basic sanitation policy setting contractual coverage targets (99% water, 90% sewage collection/treatment) -- and its political-institutional-regulatory (PIR) alignment with tariff/subsidy design and private-sector-participation incentives for vulnerable/informal-settlement households. Real national statistics: 82% WSS access (2019), 40 million without water access, 100 million without sewage access, 5+ million households across 13,000+ informal settlements (IBGE 2020). Documents fees/BURDEN (tariff and non-tariff subsidy design for low-income users), DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION (SISAR cooperative model requiring initial subsidy; contract-modeling mechanisms to reach vulnerable/informal areas), and institutional_fragmentation/political_coordination (municipal-state government alignment needed for informal-settlement service expansion).

title: Beyond water scarcity: Water (in)security and social justice in Karachi
authors: Khan H.F.; Arshad S.A.
notes: Rigorous mixed-methods study (465 household surveys across 11 Union Councils + stakeholder interviews + participant observation + water-quality testing) of water insecurity in Lyari, a semi-regularized low-income township at the tail-end of Karachi's water network. Documents a real historical ELIGIBILITY/tenure mechanism (Lyari regularized only post-1970s via 90-year government leases enabling inclusion in city water infrastructure plans) and a live administrative BURDEN mechanism: KWSB (utility) places the onus on households to self-register at revenue offices to receive billing -- 80% of connected households receive no bill, and officials attribute non-billing to lack of lease/registration or 'illegal connections' (unauthorized direct connection to supply lines). Real quantitative findings: 93% of households (n=465) have piped connections but all 33 unconnected households are in the bottom 50th income percentile; only 16% actually rely on KWSB supply day-to-day due to intermittency; households earning <5,000 PKR/month spend ~18% of income on water vs. ~2% for households earning >=40,000 PKR/month; 9% of connected households pay informal collectively-managed-supply charges on top of formal costs.

title: Piped water revenue and investment strategies in rural Africa
authors: Armstrong A.; Hope R.; Koehler J.
notes: Quantitative econometric study (GEE regression on >3,900 monthly operator revenue records from rural piped water schemes in Ghana, Rwanda, and Uganda) modeling how tariff level, connection type (on-premises vs. off-premises), and payment method (prepaid credit vs. pay-as-you-fetch vs. monthly billing) affect revenue and, by extension, affordability/economic access. Documents a real BURDEN/economic_access mechanism: on-premises connections carry an average 17% higher tariff in 3 of 4 service-area archetypes, posing 'a potential affordability risk to poorer households who may be unable to afford the up-front or ongoing cash expense', pushing them toward informal/unimproved sources; off-premises standpipes/kiosks 'do not require users to pay connection fees and enable better targeting of subsidies'. Also documents institutional/policy tension: cost-recovery tariff-setting goals often conflict with political agendas to protect poor populations, and 'poor enforcement' of payment rules is exacerbated by unpaid volunteer rural service providers lacking administrative skills. Fewer than 2 in 5 rural African households are estimated to pay for water at all (Banerjee & Morella 2011; Foster & Hope 2017, cited).

title: Analysis of the universalization, investment and governance of the sewage service of the municipal headquarters of the Easter Watershed (BHL) in Bahia; [Análise da universalização, investimento e governança do serviço de esgoto sanitário de sedes municipais das Bacias Hidrográficas do Leste (BHL) na Bahia]
authors: Carvalho J.I.C.; de Jesus Júnior G.; Gomes R.L.
notes: Quali-quantitative legal-institutional study (Brazilian law journal) of Brazil's Lei 11.445/07 (National Basic Sanitation Policy) universalization, investment, and governance principles applied to 20 municipalities in Bahia's Eastern Watersheds (Bacias Hidrograficas do Leste). Uses real SNIS (National Basic Sanitation System) and IBGE data plus formal public-records requests (e-SIC) sent to municipal governments. Real national/regional outcome statistics: only 51.92% of the Brazilian population has sewage-collection access (100+ million without it); only 44.92% of collected sewage is properly treated; in the Northeast region, only 26.76% of sewage produced is collected and only 36.22% of that is treated. Frames sanitation as a constitutional/statutory service (Arts. 175-176 Federal Constitution) and human right requiring the State to ensure universal, equitable, safe access -- directly examines the legal/administrative universalization-governance mechanism for a specific set of municipalities.

title: Modes of access to water for domestic use in rural Chile: a typological proposal
authors: Chloé N.-A.; Gustavo B.; Carlos B.; Noelia C.
notes: Mixed-methods typology study of modes of household water access in rural Chile: systematic lit review (12 papers) + quantitative analysis of national CASEN 2017 household survey (2,257,128 rural population; 53.7% networked, 46.3% not) and a consolidated national database of 2,559 rural water organizations + 5 semi-structured expert interviews. Real, analyzed legal/institutional mechanisms tied to household-level access outcomes: Law 20,998 (2019) on Rural Sanitary Services regularizing a previously unregulated sector; General Law of Sanitary Services provision that urban sanitation concessionaires are NOT required to deliver water outside their urban concession area, and neighboring APR Committees/Cooperatives are similarly not required to supply new rural housing developments -- a discretion/accommodation-type legal exclusion mechanism that drives real-estate companies to create private sanitation companies or small autonomous distribution services; Law on Real-Estate Co-ownership treatment of water systems as common domain assets financed via homeowner fees; lack of regularized water rights/land title barring 'autonomous' organizations from formal recognition, and researcher-documented cases where communities avoid formalizing specifically to escape state requirements. Outcome variables are household-level modes of water access (networked/APR/formal/autonomous/private/cistern-truck reliance), directly on this review's target outcome hierarchy. Household water/sanitation access, institutional/legal mechanism (ELIGIBILITY, DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION) analyzed with genuine quantitative national survey data plus qualitative expert validation.

title: Water insecurity in the Global North: A review of experiences in U.S. colonias communities along the Mexico border
authors: Wutich A.; Jepson W.; Velasco C.; Roque A.; Gu Z.; Hanemann M.; Hossain M.J.; Landes L.; Larson R.; Li W.W.; Morales O.; Patwoary N.; Porter S.; Tsai Y.-S.; Zheng M.; Westerhoff P.
notes: Focused/narrative review (WIREs Water, multidisciplinary author team including a law professor, Rhett Larson) synthesizing the literature on water insecurity in U.S. colonias along the Mexico border. Directly on this review's core administrative-law-mechanism thesis: identifies 'municipal underbounding' -- the intentional legal-political non-annexation of low-income minority unincorporated communities by neighboring municipalities via 'conspicuous gerrymandering' of municipal boundaries -- as a central, analyzed legal mechanism producing household-level water/sanitation exclusion. Also discusses: historical Texas 'contract for deed' property-law arrangements (unrecorded/informal land-sale contracts letting sellers avoid legal service-provision obligations until a 1989 Texas law change); the Safe Drinking Water Act's (SDWA, 40 U.S.C. section 300f et seq.) size-based regulatory classification (systems <3,300 people get lighter monitoring requirements; many colonias systems and private wells fall outside SDWA coverage entirely) as a documented regulatory-threshold mechanism producing differential water-quality protection. Real household-level outcomes cited from underlying empirical literature: cost-of-remaining-unannexed estimates ( million for a 100-resident colonia to 0 million for a colonia with thousands of residents), physical/mental health impacts. Secondary review, not primary data collection -- flagged study_design_class=systematic_review_secondary per established convention (cf. S015, S019, S027, S052), never to be pooled as an independent primary effect, but substantively central to this review's mechanism-to-outcome focus given its direct analysis of municipal underbounding and SDWA regulatory-threshold mechanisms.

title: Regulating Citywide Inclusive Sanitation (CWIS) in Colombia
authors: Saker A.; Pedraza A.B.; Narayan A.S.
notes: Qualitative case-study analysis (in-depth policy review of Colombian laws/decrees/resolutions/court rulings + semi-structured interviews + stakeholder workshops) of whether Colombia's sanitation regulatory framework enables Citywide Inclusive Sanitation (CWIS, i.e., non-sewered/onsite sanitation alternatives for underserved/informal areas). Exceptionally rich, directly analyzed legal-mechanism-to-outcome content: Law 142-1994's narrow sewered-only sanitation definition excludes onsite/shared alternatives from the regulatory scheme; Decree 1272-2017/Resolution 699-2021 create a flexible-tariff scheme for underserved areas but impose no obligation on utilities to expand to 'non formalized zones' and require a municipal certification that a zone has 'urbanization prospect' (a discretionary political-will barrier -- 'not always within the mayor's interest to formalize zones'); subsidies apply only to sewered systems, making non-sewered/informal-settlement households ineligible for financial assistance (ELIGIBILITY mechanism); funding for WSS projects nationally requires land-legality certification, creating a documentation/tenure barrier for informal settlements (DOCUMENTATION/property mechanism); Law 2044-2020 obliges local authorities to address vulnerable informal-settlement conditions via service provision or relocation, but Law 388-1997 bars service provision in high-risk zones with no interim solution while relocation (often lengthy) is pending (ENFORCEMENT/exclusion mechanism); outdated land-planning instruments (88% outdated/inaccurate) leave marginalized zones outside official planning tools, again dependent on mayoral political will. Directly on this review's core mechanism families (eligibility, documentation/tenure, discretion, enforcement) with a household/community-level sanitation-service-access outcome.

title: Experimenting with Urban–Rural Partnerships for Sustainable Sanitation in India: Learning from Practice
authors: Dasgupta S.; Agarwal N.
notes: Participatory action-research case study (authors directly supported design and implementation, 2019-2021) of India's first intergovernmental urban-rural partnership for faecal sludge management (FSM), Dhenkanal district, Odisha. Real mixed-methods data: 1,000-household rural survey, structured interviews with 8 gram panchayat sarpanchs, FSTP capacity/utilization records (27 kilolitres/day, ~50% utilized), and administrative/geospatial data. Directly analyzed institutional/legal mechanism: an informal, pre-existing market-led arrangement charged rural households 1.5-2x the urban per-trip service fee before the pilot; the pilot established a formal cooperative agreement (explicitly noted as 'an agreement and not a contract,' lacking legal enforceability equivalent to a private contract) between the urban local body and rural gram panchayats, with eligibility/service-area boundaries determined by distance thresholds and non-contiguous jurisdictional geography (gram panchayats made of scattered villages/hamlets), creating a genuine ELIGIBILITY-type boundary-determination mechanism producing 'institutionally sanctioned unequal access to services' among villages within the same jurisdiction. Documented household-level outcomes: rural households grew to 13% of all households served (Jan 2019-Feb 2020); service charges for rural households were reduced following the partnership; institutional responsibilities were clarified. Directly on this review's political_coordination/institutional_fragmentation and eligibility mechanism families with a household-level sanitation-access/affordability outcome.

title: Sanitation infrastructure at the systemic edge: Segregated roma settlements and multiple health risks in slovakia
authors: Filčák R.; Škobla D.
notes: Mixed-methods ethnographic + quantitative study of institutional discrimination against segregated Roma settlements in Slovakia (22 villages, 90 semi-structured interviews, Jan-Feb 2020) plus national quantitative data (Atlas of Roma Communities 2019, Office of Public Health Authority disease database, Ministry of Environment water/sewerage database). Genuine household-level connection outcomes: only 59% of Roma households with potential water-pipeline access are actually connected/using it (vs 76% potential); only 35% actually connected to sewerage (vs 51% potential). Disease-outbreak correlation: 85% of contagious-disease outbreak cases (4,693 cases, 2014-2018) occurred in municipalities where at least some Roma households lack water/sewerage connection. Real, analyzed legal/institutional mechanism: a three-type typology of municipal governance (rural-slum/inert, developmental, and 'not in my backyard' discriminatory) built from fieldwork, with Type C municipalities explicitly using the 'illegal' status of non-registered dwellings (Construction Authorities registration) and land-tenure/ownership barriers to justify excluding Roma settlements from sanitation-infrastructure extension while connecting non-Roma dwellings in the same village. Directly on this review's discretion/accommodation and documentation/tenure mechanism families with a household-level formal-connection/exclusion outcome -- a strong match to the dissertation's central thesis on administrative law as a mechanism of connectivity and exclusion.

title: Water rights in a time of fragility: An exploration of contestation and discourse around cape town’s “day zero” water crisis
authors: Dugard J.
notes: Law-scholar (Univ. of Witwatersrand School of Law) empirical-legal study of water rights contestation/litigation in South Africa during Cape Town's 'Day Zero' water crisis (2017-2018), based on interviews with water rights activists/lawyers over a 3-year review period (2017-2020) plus court-case and consumption-data analysis. Directly analyzes real, litigated legal-enforcement mechanisms and outcomes: Mazibuko and Others v City of Johannesburg (2009, Constitutional Court) -- the sole water rights case reaching South Africa's highest court, concerning prepaid water meters that automatically disconnected poor Phiri (Soweto) residents' water supply once an inadequate free basic water allocation was exhausted, and the constitutional adequacy of that free-basic-water quantity; Manqele v Durban Transitional Metropolitan Council (2001, unsuccessful challenge to water-service-provision sufficiency standards); Bon Vista Mansions v Southern Metropolitan Local Council (2001, established that disconnecting a household's water supply without notice/process violates constitutional due-process and section 27(1)(b) rights); a 2012 case requiring adequate water/sanitation for informal settlements; Mshengu and Others v Msunduzi Local Municipality (informal-settlement/township water provision). Real quantitative consumption-disparity data cited: townships and informal settlements consume only ~4.7-5% of a city's total water despite housing a large population share. Directly on this review's enforcement/disconnection mechanism family with household-level water-access/disconnection outcomes, grounded in genuine legal-empirical (interview + case-law) research.

title: More Sustainable Systems Through Consolidation? The Changing Landscape of Rural Drinking Water Service Delivery in Uganda
authors: Huston A.; Gaskin S.; Moriarty P.; Watsisi M.
notes: Mixed-methods systems-approach study (household and infrastructure surveys, management assessment, key informant interviews, stakeholder workshops, 2017-2019) comparing rural drinking water service delivery models (community management vs. two utility models) in Kabarole District, Uganda, during a national consolidation transition. Real, analyzed administrative-enforcement mechanism with household-level outcomes: National Water utility 'has the technical capacity to enforce payment by cutting off supply in response to non-payment,' while community-managed sources and the newer Umbrella utility lack authority/capacity to enforce tariff payment or disconnect non-compliant customers -- a documented ENFORCEMENT mechanism differing by institutional model. Household-level quantitative outcomes: only 38% of households reported paying for water regularly in 2019 (about half within National-Water-served Fort Portal municipality), 28% made ad hoc post-breakdown contributions; National Water managers reported high effective household demand for new paid connections even where free lower-service-level water was previously provided; tariffs per 20L ranged from 25 UGX (subsidised public standposts) to 94 UGX (Umbrella domestic connections). Also documents institutional fragmentation (unclear service-authority hierarchy between District Local Governments and utilities; overlapping/conflicting tariff policies within the same community) and weak legal grounding of externally introduced service models. Household connection demand, willingness-to-pay, and payment-enforcement outcomes map onto this review's enforcement/formal-connection mechanism-outcome focus.

title: Fecal sludge management system approach for establishing policy framework in urban areas of Vientiane Capital, Lao PDR
authors: Sidlakone S.; Ichiki A.
exclusion_reason_detail: Study examines the downstream fecal sludge collection/transport/treatment chain (desludging frequency, effluent BOD5/COD/TN/TP compliance, pollution loads) and government regulatory/institutional capacity to manage that chain (licensing, enforcement, institutional overlaps) -- not household-level legal/administrative barriers to obtaining a water/sanitation connection. All 230 surveyed households already have on-site sanitation facilities (flush/pour-flush toilets, septic tanks); the study's outcome is the FS treatment rate (20%->50% policy target) and environmental compliance, not household access, connection, or exclusion. Genuinely borderline given its real governance/institutional analysis content -- flagging for second-reviewer attention. Note: 8 other fecal sludge management papers already sit in this pool (search likely pulled a topical cluster) that may share this same wrong-service issue and deserve a consistent look.

title: Leveraging Artificial Intelligence for Comprehensive Analysis of Community and Rural Aqueduct Systems
authors: Salazar-Gámez L.; Ojeda-Ocaña R.; Rosero-Lombana P.; Calpa-Villarreal J.; Chañag-Checa S.; Insuasty-Enríquez J.; Cerón-Rosales A.; Garzón T.
exclusion_reason_detail: AI-driven diagnostic study of 14 community aqueduct systems in Pasto, Colombia across Technical/Environmental/Administrative-Accounting/Psychosocial dimensions. Unit of analysis is the aqueduct system (n=14), not the household -- outcomes are provider-side technical performance (WQRI, flow rates) and the provider organization's own regulatory/tax compliance (Law 142/1994, IFRS, DIAN electronic invoicing, labor formalization) rather than legal/administrative mechanisms of household access. Psychosocial component addresses internal community-governance legitimacy/participation in managing the aqueduct, not legal barriers to household connection or service access. Core contribution is a GenAI diagnostic methodology (p.900), not a legal/administrative-access study.

title: Flows against the current: governance and politics of wastewater reuse in Valle Alto, Bolivia
authors: Saldías C.; Echeverría I.; Vargas V.; Saavedra O.
exclusion_reason_detail: Strong qualitative governance/institutional-bricolage study (Saldías et al.) with rich legal analysis (Bolivia Law 1333, customary usos y costumbres, EPSA mandates) -- but the population/exposure is smallholder farmers accessing treated municipal wastewater for AGRICULTURAL IRRIGATION (p.503-511), not household connection to a networked water or sanitation service (PROJECT_SPEC.md sec7 primary outcome). Falls under INCLUSION_EXCLUSION.md exclusion criterion 7 (water-resource studies unrelated to household or community SERVICE access). Borderline given methodological fit with Family A/C moderators -- flagged for second-reviewer attention given the close call on scope (irrigation reuse vs. household drinking-water/sanitation access).

title: Financial insecurity among sanitation workers and its impacts on safe service reliability: a case study of the Arusha depot manual emptying group
authors: Kimwaga R.; Magambo H.; Ndezi T.
exclusion_reason_detail: Mixed-methods case study (financial diaries, interviews, FGDs) of the Arusha Depot Group manual pit-emptiers in Tanzania. Population/exposure is sanitation WORKERS' financial insecurity (income volatility, informal employment, lack of social protection); outcome is service reliability as mediated by worker behavior (client prioritization, delayed response, p.640-641). Households appear only as the workers' own dependents/expenditure burden, not as the population accessing a service via a legal/administrative pathway. Does not map onto this review's household/applicant unit of analysis or outcome hierarchy (PROJECT_SPEC.md sec7) -- it is a labor-economics study of the supply side of informal sanitation service delivery, not household legal/administrative access.

title: Assessing urban water security in Awash River Basin, Addis Ababa, and its surrounding towns using Integrated Urban Water S ecurity Index
authors: Legass A.M.; Alamirew T.; Gebrehiwot S.G.; Haro-Monteagudo D.; Tsegaye L.; Begashaw G.B.
exclusion_reason_detail: Composite water security index study (IUWSI/DECS framework) dominated by hydrology, water-quality chemistry (arsenic, E. coli, BOD, turbidity), GIS spatial mapping, and CMIP6 climate modeling. 'Governance' appears only as a single household-survey satisfaction item (71.3% dissatisfied with AAWSA, sec4.4/Appendix A) and generic policy-recommendation language (transboundary governance, kebele forums); no legal, administrative, or institutional access mechanism is analyzed as an exposure variable. Falls under exclusion criteria 2-4 (engineering/water-quality/hydrology study without substantive governance or access analysis).

title: Co-Creating an Intersectional Water Justice Toolkit and Documentary in Cape Town, South Africa
authors: Puvaneyshwaran D.; Logie C.H.; Van Borek S.; Abrams A.; Grootboom L.; MacKenzie F.; Taing L.; Perez-Brumer A.; Gittings L.
exclusion_reason_detail: Published under Health Promotion Practice's 'Resources, Frameworks, and Perspectives' section -- describes the co-design and components of an advocacy toolkit and 17-min documentary film ('Water Justice Alliance-Building Toolkit'), built from 10 walk-along interviews, 5 focus groups, and 2 alliance-building workshops with activists across five social movements. No outcome relevant to access, connection, service availability, reliability, quantity, affordability, or exclusion is measured or reported (INCLUSION_EXCLUSION.md criterion 4) -- the article reports on toolkit/film development and components, not empirical findings about water access determinants. A knowledge-mobilization/practice resource, not an empirical access study.

title: Effectiveness of emergency WASH strategies in disaster-prone areas of Africa: a systematic review
authors: Chirwa E.; Mwalwanda A.; Soko M.; Mbakaya B.C.
exclusion_reason_detail: Systematic review (PROSPERO CRD42024628289) of the effectiveness of emergency WASH/sanitation interventions (latrines, water treatment, chlorine sprayers) on HEALTH outcomes (cholera/disease prevention) during disasters in Africa (6 included studies). Outcome is disease incidence/health impact, not access, connection, service availability, reliability, quantity, affordability, or exclusion (PROJECT_SPEC.md sec7). No legal, administrative, institutional, or governance factor is examined as an exposure -- 'policy' appears only generically in implications-for-practice language, not as an analyzed mechanism. Wrong outcome relative to this review's hierarchy.

title: Responsible leadership and sustainability performance of health and sanitation projects: the mediating role of resilience
authors: Kyambade M.; Mwesigwa R.; Alinda K.; Tumwine S.; Lwanga F.
exclusion_reason_detail: Cross-sectional PLS-SEM survey (n=520 respondents: project managers, engineers, public health officers, M&E staff, procurement officers, beneficiary reps) across 86 health/sanitation PROJECTS in Central Uganda. Exposure is 'responsible leadership' style; mediator is organizational resilience (shock absorption, redundancy, adaptability); outcome is 'sustainability performance' (triple bottom line: economic/social/environmental viability of the PROJECT). Population is project staff/implementers, not households/applicants; outcome is organizational/project performance, not household connection, access, reliability, or affordability (PROJECT_SPEC.md sec7). No legal, administrative, or regulatory access mechanism is examined -- this is organizational-behavior/leadership scholarship, not a legal-administrative access study.

title: Water for All: A Strategic Assessment of Drinking Water Management at Cox's Bazar of Bangladesh in the Light of SDGs
authors: Molla M.H.; Chowdhury M.A.T.; Muhibbullah M.
exclusion_reason_detail: Stakeholder-perception SDG-alignment scorecard (Likert-scale agreement scores on 20 targets across 6 SDGs -- climate, urban resilience, marine, biodiversity, health, water/sanitation) plus a technical municipal water supply-demand gap calculation. Community participation (Target 6.b) is one of 20 equally-weighted Likert items, not an analyzed legal/administrative access mechanism with a measured connection/access outcome; administrative/bureaucratic/political barriers appear only as a minor category (~8% combined) in a household 'key challenges' figure dominated by budget/technical/salinity factors. No specific legal, administrative, institutional, or regulatory mechanism is traced against a household-level access outcome -- this is a needs-assessment/SDG-scorecard study, not a legal-administrative access study.

title: Exploring the role of institutional governance in enhancing sustainability performance of health and sanitation projects in Uganda: a qualitative inquiry
authors: Kyambade M.; Mwesigwa R.; Alinda K.; Tumwine S.; Lwanga F.
exclusion_reason_detail: Qualitative institutional-theory inquiry (21 interviews with policymakers, health officers, and project managers) into how governance (policies, regulatory frameworks, organizational structures) shapes the 'sustainability performance' (economic/social/environmental continuity beyond donor funding) of health/sanitation PROJECTS in Uganda. Population is project-level stakeholders/implementers, not households/applicants; outcome is organizational/project continuity and legitimacy (institutional isomorphism framing), not household connection, access, reliability, or affordability (PROJECT_SPEC.md sec7). Same scope issue as the related R4F8CFC42FFE1 (Kyambade et al., responsible leadership) already excluded from this same author cluster -- this is donor-project governance/organizational-sustainability scholarship, not a household legal-administrative access study.

title: The Agency, Resources, and Institutional Structures for Sanitation-related Empowerment (ARISE) scales: Psychometric evaluation across eight cities in Asia and Africa
authors: Sinharoy S.S.; Xia D.; Patrick M.; McManus S.; Chipungu J.; Reddy Y.M.; Ahmed T.; Mink T.; Pan Y.; Bhan T.; Conrad A.; Caruso B.A.
exclusion_reason_detail: Psychometric scale-validation study (EFA/CFA, measurement invariance, composite reliability, test-retest reliability) of the ARISE scales measuring 16 sub-domains of women's sanitation-related empowerment (agency, resources, institutional structures as social/psychological constructs) across 5,586 women in 8 cities. The outcome measured is scale psychometric performance, not household connection, access, reliability, quantity, or affordability (PROJECT_SPEC.md sec7). 'Institutional structures' here denotes a perceived-norms empowerment sub-construct, not a specific legal/administrative/regulatory access mechanism. An instrument-development/methods paper, not an empirical access study. Related ARISE cluster papers already in the pool (RACC1A9A71A20 development/validation, RB76A3B41BBBF protocol, R3A595AC61767 mental well-being) likely share this issue and are not yet screened; R6AC58735B46B (the underlying systematic review/qualitative metasynthesis feeding the ARISE framework) may differ and warrants separate assessment.

title: Does Economic Growth Drive Equitable Water and Sanitation Access? Assessing Inequality Reduction Across 64 Nations
authors: García-López M.; López-Ruiz S.; Cuadrado-Quesada G.
exclusion_reason_detail: Cross-country econometric panel study (OLS/2SLS/SURE) of 64 nations testing whether GDP-per-capita growth reduces inequality in aggregate JMP basic water/sanitation access rates (by income quintile and urban/rural), with Gini, inflation, water-use efficiency, schooling, economic complexity, and a generic 'governance effectiveness' index (a World-Bank-style macro governance-quality score) as covariates. Unit of analysis is the country (n=64), not the household; outcome is national/urban/rural aggregate access-rate inequality (standard deviation across quintiles), not an individual household's connection/access/reliability/affordability status. 'Governance effectiveness' is a generic macro-governance quality index, not a specific legal/administrative access mechanism mapping onto this review's mechanism framework (ELIGIBILITY/BURDEN/DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION/ENFORCEMENT, PROJECT_SPEC.md sec6). Core research question is macroeconomic (growth-inequality nexus), not administrative-law/legal-mechanism. Borderline given the paper's explicit finding that governance effectiveness outpredicts income inequality -- flagged for second-reviewer attention.

title: Enablers and Obstacles in Integrated Water Resources Management (IWRM) Implementation and Their Contributions to Sustainable Territorial Development
authors: Gallegos A.; Grigg N.S.; Llano W.
exclusion_reason_detail: PRISMA systematic review of 375 empirical articles on Integrated Water Resources Management (IWRM) implementation enablers/obstacles, coded at basin, sub-basin, transboundary, urban, and national scales, linked to 'Sustainable Territorial Development' outcomes (economic productivity, ecosystem integrity, governance legitimacy). Unit of analysis throughout is the IWRM implementation case/institution/basin, not the household -- no household-level connection, access, reliability, or affordability outcome is examined anywhere in the review (PROJECT_SPEC.md sec7). Institutional/legal/regulatory frameworks are discussed as one of ten enabler categories (25% prevalence), but always as a driver of basin-scale resource-management effectiveness, not household service access. Falls under INCLUSION_EXCLUSION.md exclusion criterion 7 (water-resource studies unrelated to household or community service access).

title: Water Security in Fragile States: Mapping Governance and Water Access in Libya
authors: Ellinport B.; Galaitsi S.E.; Pavur G.; Baher A.; Marcellin M.C.; Lambert J.H.; Trump B.D.; Linkov I.
exclusion_reason_detail: GIS-based composite water security index (natural-availability axis + infrastructure-investment axis) across Libya's 22 districts, built entirely from secondary/aggregated data (precipitation, desalination/dam/wastewater-plant capacity, GMMR network reliance %, electricity access) -- no primary household survey or interview data was collected by the authors. 'Governance' functions as thematic framing (fragile state legitimacy, infrastructure investment as a proxy for 'trust in government') rather than a specific legal/administrative access mechanism (eligibility, connection procedure, enforcement) examined against measured household-level access variation. This is a risk-analysis/systems-engineering framework paper for prioritizing infrastructure investment, comparable in structure to the already-excluded Legass et al. Awash River Basin composite index (R1B34F60D5F79).

title: REVISITING: Off-grid, the New Water Supply Solution
authors: Gaudry A.; Colon M.; Baron C.
exclusion_reason_detail: Narrative/critical policy book chapter (edited-volume format with 'Further Readings'/'Selected References' sections) synthesizing existing secondary literature and World Bank reports on 'off-grid' water solutions -- discusses regulatory challenges, governance fragmentation, and equity concerns narratively via illustrative case citations (Dakar, Bandung, Cambodia, Cochabamba, Dar es Salaam, Kolkata), but presents no primary empirical data of its own and no systematic review methodology (one informal conference-sideline interview footnote is not a research method). Does not satisfy INCLUSION_EXCLUSION.md criterion 3 (empirical evidence or systematic empirical synthesis) as a standalone study.

title: Drinking Water Quality Regulations: A Contrast Between Germany and Latin America
authors: Vogelmann E.S.; Prevedello J.; Tiruneh G.A.
exclusion_reason_detail: Comparative documentary/doctrinal analysis of drinking-water QUALITY regulations (chemical/microbiological Maximum Allowable Values -- E. coli, turbidity, fluoride, nitrate, arsenic, lead, microcystin-LR, Water Safety Plan adoption) across Latin American countries, Mexico, Cuba, and Germany/EU. Unit of analysis is the national legal/regulatory text (de jure standards), not households; outcome is regulatory stringency/content divergence, not household connection, access, reliability, or affordability (PROJECT_SPEC.md sec7). No household-level empirical access data. Governance/institutional-capacity theory (multilevel governance) is used only to explain WHY regulatory stringency differs across countries, not as a mechanism examined against a household access outcome. Matches exclusion criteria 1 (doctrinal/comparative-law analysis without empirical access evidence) and 3 (water-quality study, not access).

title: Institutional trust as a critical determinant of households’ willingness to pay for improved water services in Leku Town, Ethiopia
authors: Dumo W.M.
exclusion_reason_detail: Cross-sectional contingent valuation survey (n=193 households, binary logistic regression) of willingness to pay (WTP) for improved water services in Leku Town, Ethiopia. 'Institutional trust' and 'service satisfaction' are operationalized as attitudinal/perceptual survey items (attitude toward the water provider, satisfaction with service timing), not a specific legal, administrative, or regulatory access mechanism (eligibility, connection procedure, licensing, enforcement) examined empirically. Outcome is hypothetical WTP (a demand-economics/contingent-valuation construct used for tariff design), not household connection, access, reliability, or actual affordability/expenditure burden (PROJECT_SPEC.md sec7) -- 'Do not pool these simply because they all use the word access.' A related Nepal WTP study (R4D38A1953C24, Dhanusk et al.) is also in the pool and likely shares this issue; not yet screened.

title: Water, Sanitation and Health: The World Bank's Financing of Sustainable Development Goal 6
authors: Martínez-Gómez C.; Gallego-Valero L.; Moral-Pajares E.
exclusion_reason_detail: Descriptive-comparative macro analysis of 546 World Bank water/sanitation financing projects (2000-2022) using secondary data (World Bank project records, WHO access-indicator percentages, a Government Effectiveness index, child mortality rates). Unit of analysis is the country/project, not the household; outcome is aggregate national financing allocation and country-level access-percentage improvement, not an individual household's connection/access/reliability/affordability status (PROJECT_SPEC.md sec7). 'Governance conditions' is a generic macro Government Effectiveness index limiting country borrowing capacity, not a specific legal/administrative mechanism examined against household-level access variation -- structurally comparable to the already-excluded García-López et al. (R5E653CCC67DF) and Gallegos et al. (R2D6E5154CE63) cross-country/macro analyses.

title: Knowledge, economic, and WASH challenges affecting menstrual health and hygiene among nursing students in Bangladesh using a mixed-methods approach
authors: Zaman M.N.U.; Sai A.; Yamauchi T.
exclusion_reason_detail: Mixed-methods study (n=370 survey + 6 FGDs) of menstrual health and hygiene (MHH) among nursing/midwifery students across seven government colleges in Bangladesh. Population is nursing students in institutional educational settings, not households/applicants seeking water or sanitation service connection. Outcome variables are MHH indicators (adequate menstrual materials, WASH facility adequacy for menstrual management, menstrual knowledge, health impact, social support, discomfort) -- WASH facility adequacy is one of six outcomes and concerns campus-level menstrual-management conditions, not household connection, access, reliability, or affordability (PROJECT_SPEC.md sec7). No legal, administrative, institutional, or regulatory water/sanitation access mechanism is examined; policy context (2016 National Curriculum, Water and Sanitation Sector Development Plan) appears only as background, not as an analyzed exposure.

title: Hydro-citizenship revisited: water, belonging, and the politics of adaptation in rough neighbourhoods in the Global South
authors: Bhanye J.
exclusion_reason_detail: Theoretical/conceptual 'Short Communication' re-theorizing 'hydro-citizenship' through political ecology and Southern urban theory, drawing loosely on ~2 years of the author's own ethnographic engagement (field visits, walk-alongs, community workshops) in Cape Town flood-prone settlements, illustrated with secondary examples from Dhaka, Nairobi, Jakarta, and Lagos. The paper's own empirical grounding concerns flood-response practices (trench digging, WhatsApp alerts, clean-ups), not water/sanitation service access specifically; water/sanitation-specific barriers (intermittent supply, illegal-connection policing, metering/affordability) are named in a single passage citing another source (Mgwele et al. 2024, already in this pool as R10949E2F3E33 and worth screening directly) rather than the author's own data. Does not provide enough information to identify a specific water/sanitation population, exposure, and outcome per INCLUSION_EXCLUSION.md criterion 5 -- borderline given genuine ethnographic grounding on the broader adaptation-citizenship theme; flagged for second-reviewer attention.

title: ‘No Human Entry’ on Paper: Outsourcing Labour, Implementation Gaps, and Everyday Illegality of Manual Scavenging in India
authors: Raj N.; Tiwari M.
exclusion_reason_detail: Secondary-source analysis (legislation, court rulings, surveys, reports, media accounts) of the persistence of manual scavenging in India despite the MS Acts of 1993/2013, using Braverman's labour process theory and Burawoy's manufacturing consent to explain caste-based occupational exploitation of Dalit sanitation WORKERS. Population/exposure is manual scavengers' labor conditions (informal contracting, deskilling, bureaucratic outsourcing, rebranding as 'Safai Mitras'); outcome is persistence of exploitative sanitation labor and caste oppression, not household water/sanitation SERVICE access, connection, reliability, or affordability (PROJECT_SPEC.md sec7). Legal/enforcement analysis (MS Act, Supreme Court rulings in Safai Karmachari Andolan v. Union of India and Dr. Balram Singh v. Union of India) is substantively examined but directed at labor-rights/occupational-safety enforcement for sanitation workers, not household access to a sanitation service -- same population mismatch as the already-excluded Kimwaga et al. (R15EF22174A64, Arusha sanitation workers).

title: Optimal water tariffs and trade-offs: a multi-objective analysis of municipalities in Pernambuco; [Tarifas ótimas de água e compensações: uma análise multiobjetivo dos municípios de Pernambuco]
authors: De Lima e Silva A.; De Lima e Silva Y.C.; Alcoforado de Moraes M.M.G.
exclusion_reason_detail: Multi-objective optimization model (nonlinear programming solved via GAMS/CONOPT, 3,444 equations/4,131 variables) generating a Pareto frontier of optimal water tariffs across 172 municipalities in Pernambuco, Brazil, balancing utility revenue against a modeled affordability constraint (household income by consumer category from the 2010 IBGE Census). Unit of analysis is the municipality/consumer-category aggregate, not the household; outcome is a normative/prescriptive tariff-design solution set (simulated trade-offs), not an observed household connection, access, reliability, or affordability outcome (PROJECT_SPEC.md sec7). References to regulatory context (State Law No. 12,427/2003, national sanitation targets) are background, not an empirically examined legal/administrative access mechanism. This is an operations-research/economic-modeling paper for tariff policy design, not an empirical access study.

title: Institutional conflicts of interest in regional water management: a case study of the water supply in the Taipei metropolitan area
authors: Chen C.-Y.; Cai Y.-S.; Hung Y.-J.; You G.J.-Y.
exclusion_reason_detail: Deterministic WEAP scenario-based hydro-economic simulation of the Taipei metropolitan multi-reservoir water supply system. Exposure/outcome are utility-level pricing, inter-basin transfer-payment mechanisms, and system-wide social loss/shortage under hydrological stress scenarios -- an engineering/economic optimization study, not an empirical household-level access study. Household affordability burden is raised only as a policy-implications discussion point in the conclusion, not measured as data or an outcome variable.

title: Governance, structure, and access: a Bayesian hierarchical analysis of water, sanitation, and hygiene in South Asia
authors: Azimi M.N.; Rahman M.M.
exclusion_reason_detail: Country-level panel analysis (Bayesian hierarchical linear model, 8 South Asian countries, 2000-2024, World Development Indicators data); unit of analysis is the country, not the household. 'Governance' is a composite autoencoder-derived index built from six generic Worldwide Governance Indicators dimensions (voice/accountability, regulatory quality, political stability, control of corruption, government effectiveness, rule of law), not a specific legal/administrative access mechanism (eligibility, burden, discretion, or enforcement) tied to household-level outcomes. Same cross-country composite-governance-index pattern as the earlier-excluded García-López (R5E653CCC67DF) and Gallegos (R2D6E5154CE63) papers.

title: Resilience and Sustainability Performance of Health and Sanitation Projects in Uganda
authors: Kyambade M.; Mwesigwa R.; Alinda K.; Tumwine S.; Lwanga F.
exclusion_reason_detail: PLS-SEM survey (n=520 stakeholders: project staff, procurement/technical officers, regulatory officials, beneficiary reps) across 86 health/sanitation projects in Uganda; exposure is organizational resilience (shock absorption, adaptability, redundancy, learning/innovation), outcome is project-level 'sustainability performance' (economic efficiency, social outcomes, environmental management) -- not household-level legal/administrative water/sanitation access. Third paper in the Kyambade et al. project-management cluster (see also R4F8CFC42FFE1, R26FD0045CAAA), same wrong-population/wrong-outcome issue.

title: A Systematic Overview of Institutional Pathways and Constraints in the Integration of Local and Indigenous Knowledge into Water Resource Policy: An African Perspective
authors: Ngubane Z.; Aliyu Yaro N.S.; Ziqubu S.M.; Adedeji J.A.
exclusion_reason_detail: Explicitly interpretive/conceptual thematic synthesis of 30 studies (authors state they do not follow formal PRISMA methodology); unit of analysis is institutional/governance systems (rhetorical recognition, legal marginalisation, participatory/co-management frameworks, state-led authority) across Africa generally, not households. No household-level water/sanitation access, connection, reliability, affordability, or administrative outcome is measured or synthesized anywhere. Same no-household-outcome pattern as the earlier-excluded Gallegos IWRM review (R2D6E5154CE63) and García-López cross-country panel (R5E653CCC67DF).

title: Examining awareness, implementation, and challenges of sustainable development goal 6 in rural Osun State, Nigeria
authors: Ogunbode T.O.; Awolola V.O.
exclusion_reason_detail: Household survey (n=310, 31 rural communities, Osun State, Nigeria) whose measured outcome, via factor analysis, is respondents' 'awareness of SDG 6' -- not a formal connection, effective/economic access, or administrative access outcome. Exposure factors identified (cultural beliefs about water as a communal resource, poverty, poor road connectivity, poor women's empowerment programming) drive awareness, not a legal/administrative access mechanism. Descriptive statistics on MDG-era borehole presence/functionality by community are purely infrastructure-maintenance data (non-functional due to poor maintenance/lack of technical expertise), with no eligibility, application, discretion, or enforcement process analyzed as an exposure variable.

title: Barriers to water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) cluster coordination during emergencies in sub-Saharan Africa: A scoping review
authors: Yimenu A.A.; Gemechu M.T.; Shimber E.T.; Ndugga P.
exclusion_reason_detail: JBI scoping review (39 studies) of barriers to inter-agency WASH humanitarian cluster coordination in sub-Saharan Africa emergencies. Unit of analysis is the coordination cluster/humanitarian agency, not the household; outcomes are funding continuity, local capacity, monitoring/accountability systems, and coordination effectiveness -- no household-level access, connection, reliability, affordability, or administrative access outcome is synthesized anywhere. Same emergency-WASH-effectiveness pattern as the earlier-excluded Chirwa review (R50C907E99BA5), one level further removed (agency coordination rather than health outcomes).

title: Beyond access: WASH, public health, and sustainable development priorities in Africa—a narrative review
authors: Elmi A.H.; Ibrahim R.K.
exclusion_reason_detail: Explicitly a narrative review, not a systematic review -- authors state no formal quality appraisal or structured search strategy was undertaken and acknowledge this limits rigor. Continent-wide (Africa) thematic synthesis of WASH inequalities, public health burden, and generic governance/infrastructure/financing barriers, with no specific legal/administrative access mechanism analyzed and no household-level outcome data synthesized. Does not meet INCLUSION_EXCLUSION.md criterion 3's 'systematic empirical synthesis' standard; same no-household-outcome, too-broad-scope pattern as the earlier-excluded Ngubane LIK review (R6E8BD60B13E0) and Gallegos IWRM review (R2D6E5154CE63).

title: A Qualitative Exploration of Social Sustainability Performance in Health and Sanitation Projects
authors: Kyambade M.; Mwesigwa R.; Alinda K.; Tumwine S.; Lwanga F.
exclusion_reason_detail: Qualitative exploratory study (21 semi-structured interviews with community members, local council leaders, and project implementers) in central Uganda; outcome is 'social sustainability performance' of health/sanitation projects (meaningful participation, trust-building, perceived fairness, community-led maintenance, social cohesion), not household-level legal/administrative water/sanitation access. Fourth and final paper in the Kyambade et al. project-management cluster (see also R4F8CFC42FFE1, R26FD0045CAAA, R5FB1EE86B250), same wrong-population/wrong-outcome issue.

title: Drinking Water Supply Strategies for Archipelagic States: Scale-Constrained Systems and Off-Grid Solutions from Small Islands in Indonesia
authors: Plamonia N.; Purnama R.A.; Novitasari Y.; Rosya E.; Mulyono H.; Firmansyah R.; Purwanta W.; Trisnoharjono D.B.; Nuridha A.; Mardiyana I.; Wati S.; Setiawan A.; Raharjo S.; Putri R.D.
exclusion_reason_detail: Comparative mixed-evidence engineering/economic feasibility study (secondary data, limited field verification) of off-grid drinking water systems across 15 small Indonesian islands. Household cost/expenditure data exists, but the paper's own explicit research-question framing (RQ-2) concludes that 'service failure reflects structural scale incompatibility rather than institutional weakness' -- the authors deliberately reject an institutional/administrative explanation for the access gap in favor of a purely physical/hydrogeological/demographic scale-mismatch explanation. No legal/administrative mechanism (eligibility, burden, discretion, or enforcement) is analyzed as an exposure variable. Same engineering/technical-feasibility pattern as the earlier-excluded Legass, Ellinport, and Chen (Taipei WEAP) papers.

title: A review of the drivers and barriers influencing the impact of Water, Sanitation and Hygiene on attendance and retention of pupils in primary schools in developing countries
authors: Adekunle E.; Ottoh F.; Osimen G.; Akinola A.
exclusion_reason_detail: Narrative review (Mini Review, not systematic; literature search 2015-2025) of drivers/barriers of WASH's impact on school attendance and retention of pupils in developing-country primary schools. Population is pupils/schools, not households; outcome is educational attendance/retention, not household-level water/sanitation access, connection, reliability, affordability, or administrative outcome. No legal/administrative access mechanism analyzed. Same wrong-population pattern as the earlier-excluded Zaman menstrual-health nursing-student study (R762C6673156D) and Sinharoy ARISE psychometrics study (R8AC9D969EC05); same non-systematic narrative-review pattern as Elmi & Ibrahim (RF7BD856CF4EE).

title: Assessing disaster vulnerability in an informal settlement of Cape Town, South Africa, through the MOVE framework
authors: Kunguma O.; Awah L.S.; Petersen I.; Lunga W.
exclusion_reason_detail: Mixed-methods disaster-vulnerability study (125-household survey, transect walks, field observations) applying the MOVE framework (exposure/susceptibility/resilience to floods and fires) in an informal settlement of Khayelitsha, Cape Town. Sanitation access (94% lacking private sanitation) is examined only as one susceptibility indicator among many (poverty, housing, unemployment, health, institutional capacity) within the disaster-vulnerability framework, not as the focal outcome. No specific legal/administrative water/sanitation access mechanism (eligibility, connection process, discretion, or enforcement) is analyzed as an exposure variable; the paper's outcome is disaster vulnerability, not household water/sanitation access.

title: The Economics of Household Water Access: A Review and Research Roadmap for "Water for All"
authors: Choumert-Nkolo J.; Phélinas P.
exclusion_reason_detail: Invited Annual Review narrative synthesis (explicitly distinguished by the authors from prior 'systematic reviews and meta-analyses' on water access, with no defined search strategy or inclusion criteria of its own). The paper's contribution is a critique of water-access measurement metrics and a call to combine quantitative (RCT-dominated) and qualitative evaluation methods for water interventions -- a methodological/research-roadmap argument, not an empirical synthesis of legal/administrative access mechanisms. Governance, tenure, and legal barriers are mentioned only in brief, citation-driven passing references, never analyzed as a specific mechanism tied to a measured household-level outcome.

title: NAVIGATING INDIA’S LEGAL GOVERNANCE IN WATER SECTOR: A SCRUTINY INTO NATIONAL PERFORMANCE UNDER SDG FRAMEWORK FOR CLEAN AND WASTEWATER MANAGEMENT IN INDIA
authors: Pegu K.; Samal K.P.
exclusion_reason_detail: Pure doctrinal legal commentary (per INCLUSION_EXCLUSION.md exclusion criterion 1) analyzing India's legal/institutional water governance architecture (Jal Jeevan Mission, AMRUT, Swachh Bharat Mission Urban) against SDG 6 targets, without empirical household-level access evidence.
